item.title: Savoring Happy Moments Together Strengthens Couples
item.description:
Relationships

Savoring Happy Moments Together Strengthens Couples

New research shows reliving our happiest moments helps relationship satisfaction.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Joint savoring—reliving happy moments together—boosts relationship satisfaction and resilience.
  • Joint savoring buffers relationships against stress, helping partners feel less defined by challenges.
  • Couples who jointly revisit positive memories report less conflict and greater confidence together.
Source: Migma__Agency/Shutterstock

Most relationship advice focuses on creating positive experiences together: date nights, vacations, shared hobbies, or meaningful conversations. But new research suggests that what matters just as much is what couples do after those moments have passed.

Joint savoring is the practice of intentionally revisiting and appreciating positive experiences together. Rather than simply remembering a great vacation or laughing about a funny moment independently, joint savoring involves partners reliving those memories together, talking about them, appreciating what they meant, and allowing the positive emotions to resurface.

A recent study introduces joint savoring as a distinct relationship process, one that goes beyond the well-established psychological concept of savoring, which has traditionally been viewed as an individual skill. Savoring refers to our ability to notice, appreciate, and extend positive emotions associated with past, present, or anticipated experiences. Joint savoring asks a different question: What happens when two people savor the same experience together?

The researchers surveyed 589 adults in romantic relationships, measuring how often couples intentionally reflected on shared positive experiences. Importantly, they controlled for personality traits like optimism, as well as each person’s general tendency to savor positive events. Even after accounting for those factors, joint savoring predicted stronger relationship functioning. Couples who engaged in it reported greater relationship satisfaction, more confidence in their future together, less conflict during communication, better overall health, higher quality of life, and lower psychological distress.

Interestingly, the research also examined stress: Stress is one of the most reliable predictors of relationship strain. Yet couples who frequently engaged in joint savoring appeared more resilient. While savoring did not eliminate the effects of stress altogether, it helped preserve relationship confidence and buffered some stress that typically accompanies stressful periods. In other words, couples who regularly revisited what was going well seemed less likely to let external pressures define their relationship.

Why Does Joint Savoring Work?

The findings align with broader theories of relationship maintenance, which suggest that thriving relationships are built not only by solving problems but also by intentionally strengthening positive emotional bonds. Shared recollection may reinforce a couple’s identity—“this is who we are together”—while reminding partners of their competence, affection, and history of overcoming challenges. Positive experiences become emotional resources that can be drawn upon during difficult times rather than fleeting moments that disappear once they’re over.

The practical implications are surprisingly simple. Instead of asking your partner, “How was your day?” consider asking, “Remember when we…” Flip through old photos. Revisit a favorite restaurant. Tell the story of how you met. Laugh about a travel story.

Happiness in relationships may not depend solely on making more memories. It may also depend on returning to the ones you’ve already made and experiencing them together all over again.

item.title: What Birds Teach Us About Stress and Resilience
item.description:
Resilience

What Birds Teach Us About Stress and Resilience

How to stop living on fumes and build real “stopover” space in your life.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Birds survive high metabolic stress through reliable “stopover sites” and routines that let them refuel.
  • Humans often live like hummingbirds, with no reserves and constant demands.
  • Resilience depends on making space for protected pockets of time and place for rest, presence, and refueling.

Next time you wake up and hear birds chirping outside your window, take a moment before you reach for your phone. Listen. It’s a bit of a miracle they survived the night at all.

Birds live closer to the edge than most of us realize. Some tiny songbirds can lose around 10 percent of their body weight overnight. Hummingbirds wake up with essentially no fat reserves. Long‑distance migrants depend on carefully packed fat stores to cross oceans or continents. For them, “running on empty” isn’t a metaphor. It’s their daily reality.

In my recent conversation with evolutionary biologist Joan Strassmann about The Social Lives of Birds on the Wild Connection podcast, we talked about what it means to live that precariously, and why, despite their vulnerability, birds somehow keep showing up at our feeders, on power lines, and in forests as if it’s no big deal. It is a big deal. And with everything we’re throwing at them, from habitat loss to noise and climate shifts, it’s getting harder for many species to keep pulling this off.

A man, a bird, and a paper bag

You might be wondering how we know birds are losing that much weight overnight. It all started with a researcher, a bird, and a paper bag. The researcher was Dr. Alan Patterson. It wasn’t idle curiosity that drove him to design this experiment. It was a way to understand how much stress short‑term handling and holding for banding added on top of what birds already endure at night. By comparing “normal overnight” metabolic costs to shorter holding periods, Patterson and others could see just how much energy a small bird burns simply by being alive in the dark. The answer was startling: that roughly 10 percent loss in body mass, night after night.

If you’re tempted to think, “Well, why don’t they just eat more and pack on a few extra?” the answer, of course, is flight.

This perilous balance is tough even for the larger end of small birds. But imagine the tiniest among them: hummingbirds. These are extreme animals in many ways. Their heart rate and wing beats alone are extraordinary. And then there are their energy reserves. By morning, they have none. They’re living on fumes. If they don’t eat quickly after they wake, they will not survive.

Hummingbirds are a useful mirror for us. They don’t have the luxury of pretending they’re fine. There’s no “powering through” to answer a few more emails. Their first behavior is self‑maintenance, not productivity. They refuel or they crash.

What about birds that aren’t small? Surely, they’re doing better. Those Canada geese waddling around ponds can look positively chunky. They may look “fat,” but a Canada goose weighs only about 6–14 pounds, and even that range is partly about migration. Birds have hollow bones (flightless species keep more solid ones, but in flying birds hollow architecture dominates), and the chest is where fat reserves are stored. That hefty breast is about survival, not a sign of indulgence.

And it’s not just large birds taking on massive journeys. Take the Connecticut warbler. It weighs a little over half an ounce (about 15 grams). Before migration, it packs on roughly an extra quarter ounce of fat. Then it leaves northern forests, travels east toward New England, and makes a grueling non‑stop ocean flight across the Atlantic and Caribbean directly into the Amazon Basin. Twice a year. Some of us can barely manage the jet lag between New York and California. This little bird is essentially flying its own red‑eye across an ocean, on a fat tank that would fit inside a teaspoon.

Here’s the catch: when you live at the edge like this, tiny extra stresses can have outsized consequences. A cold snap, a missing food patch, a destroyed stopover site, a change in wind, any of these can blow birds off course or turn a survivable night into a lethal one.

At this point, you might be saying, “Well, that’s all very interesting, but what does that have to do with us?” I’m always thinking about how other animals offer us lessons, whether directly or indirectly. Birds show us a very clear one: living on fumes is survivable only when the world still offers you places to refuel. We are living more like hummingbirds with no reserves and constant demands, while simultaneously destroying our own stopover sites. We tend to talk about resilience as if it’s an individual trait: grit, toughness, “doing it all.” Birds remind us that resilience is relational.

They survive because the world still provides food patches, roosts, and migration stopovers. When those disappear, even “tough” species crash. In human terms, resilience is less about heroics and more about infrastructure. To me, it looks like people you can lean on, things that genuinely restore you, and routines that offer reliable stability in a chaotic and unpredictable world. Our lives need these equivalents of roosts and stopover sites built in before the storm, not improvised mid‑flight when we’re already exhausted.

Birds don’t have the luxury of ignoring their energy state. If they don’t eat, they die. We do have that luxury, and we abuse it. We push through exhaustion, chronic stress, lack of restorative sleep, and emotional depletion as if we’re infinitely buffered. If your internal hummingbird is waking up with no reserves (especially in the middle of the night), that’s not a badge of honor. That’s an alarm and we should treat is as such.

We can’t avoid stress any more than birds can avoid overnight weight loss. But unlike birds, many of us pretend we’re not running on fumes. The metaphor isn’t “be more resilient like birds.” It’s “stop treating chronic depletion as normal before you break.”

Being on the edge isn’t a lifestyle (for us)

For birds, the edge is a physics problem: small body, high metabolism, flight. They didn’t choose this. It’s a byproduct of evolution. We, on the other hand, often turn the edge into a lifestyle and then an identity. Always busy, always hustling, always “on.” Some people even wear it as a badge or use it as a status symbol: “Oh, I’m just so so busy!”

But here’s the thing: we get to choose not to live like that. Save the “pack on fat and go all‑in” mode for true crossings. When there is an illness, or for caregiving, major deadlines, and real crises. Can we please start refusing to treat daily life as a permanent emergency?

Those stopover sites that migrants rely on don’t look special on the surface. They’re often just small patches of habitat where birds do something very social‑media‑unfriendly: eat and rest.

Our equivalents are things we usually describe as boring or indulgent: sleep, unstructured time, relationships that aren’t networking, walks without headphones, practices like slow birding or simply watching a squirrel on a morning walk. These are biologically important. They are our true habitat. The least glamorous parts of your life are probably the ones keeping you alive. Guard them the way a warbler guards a good patch of insects.

So the next time you hear birds at dawn, remember that most of them have just burned through 10 percent of their body weight staying alive in the dark, and now they’re doing the obvious thing. Celebrating that they’re awake and refueling.

Ask yourself: Where in your life are you waking up like a hummingbird and still expecting yourself to fly across an ocean?

And then, instead of pushing harder, see if you can build one small, unglamorous stopover site this week. Enforce a boundary. Take a nap. Take a walk in nature. Have a conversation that doesn’t revolve around productivity. These are the things that help you land, eat metaphorically, and live to sing another day.

item.title: Why Oversharing Costs More Than You Think
item.description:
Relationships

Why Oversharing Costs More Than You Think

Sharing too little beats sharing too much.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Revealing personal details builds bridges; the problem is oversharing.
  • Knowing where that line begins and ends is a critical judgment call.
  • Be more cautious about with whom you share what matters most.
Source: Nuala Walsh, AI-generated with ChatGPT/OpenAI

“Did I say too much?” you panic. Maybe it doesn’t matter if you didn’t click on a date. But what if you’re at an interview? “Did I say enough?” Or at the office party, you reveal your crush on the boss or controversial opinions on strategy. Stakes are climbing. Regret and anxiety follow.

Now it matters.

In any social, political, or workplace situation, there’s a fine line between articulating too much and too little. What is the right amount of personal disclosure and professional discretion?

Has it gone too far in today’s reveal-all culture? And does it put you at higher risk in a cancellation world?

A Rising Disclosure Trend

There’s a growing assumption that others crave to learn your inner secrets and opinions. After all, reality TV is booming. We’ve all read the LinkedIn openers, “I don’t normally share this kind of thing...” followed by revelations about everything from their dog to their addiction or trauma. The feed has become a confessional.

To what end, one might ask? For genuine advice or a virality play? When people post, they seek recognition. It’s the nature of the medium. We know that extreme, negative, or novel news commands greater attention. So regardless of content, you’re already sharing.

The impulse has roots in Brené Brown’s TED talk on "The Power of Vulnerability." She urges us to shed the need for certainty, self-sufficiency, and control, arguing that sharing deepens connection and reveals authenticity.

It’s no different at an organisation level where silence isn’t always an option. It’s legally prohibitive to hide disclosures about potential risks. It’s why medical, agri, and food products carry information labels and warnings. Yet disclosure carries a price, capable of losing millions in revenue and damaging reputation.

German pharmaceutical and agro-chemical group Bayer has spent years fighting litigation over whether Roundup, its glyphosate weedkiller, causes cancer. Should it have warned users? The science is contested. Bayer disputes the claims but set aside $16 billion to settle cases.

The Assumed Benefits of Disclosure

Professor Leslie John argues that most of us chronically under-share, and that the connection we forfeit costs more than the occasional cringe. She argues that sharing builds rapport, enhances likability, and brings people closer together. Intuitively, few would disagree. But it’s only true under certain conditions. It depends. Let’s consider each in turn.

  • Build rapport: It makes networking easier if the counterpart talks openly rather than bleats superficially. You can build rapport with someone who simply goes to the same school, lives in the same town, or shares a birthday or your name. You don’t need to know that they spent time in prison or have been adopted.
  • Enhance likability: Are talkable people more popular and trustworthy? That depends. Hearing about a brave deed can boost trust. You see others more favorably and appreciate their courage, even interpreting it as a signal of warmth toward you. For instance, the singer Lewis Capaldi openly admitted mental health issues and stepped back from performing. A high-stakes call. How does the recipient fan deal with this revelation? It can evoke pity or even change the relationship dynamic.
  • Deepen connection: Sometimes, revelations are made deliberately. A parent might choose to disclose their early experiences to an insecure teenager to deepen a bond. A presenter may open with a vulnerable anecdote to draw empathy. It becomes part of the performance. Equally, sharing is expected in dating to establish if any connection exists.
article continues after advertisement

With any of this, the trick is timing, appropriateness, and the other party's readiness to hear it.

Undersharing and oversharing aren't equal errors. One is recoverable, the other isn't. Say too little, and you can always say more. Say too much, and there's no taking it back. The upside of disclosure is real but slow. The downside is rarer but can be severe and swift. Authority weakens, leverage drops, and social judgment hardens.

3 Rules for Getting the Balance Right

People suffer more than we think when the cringe elongates. Paranoia and self-esteem issues can set in. What are the costs? What type of oversharing is really appropriate? As a behavioral scientist, I suggest three rules.

  1. Know your audience. Ask if this revelation is more likely to alienate you or deepen the connection. A misjudgment makes everyone feel uncomfortable. You squirm as your colleague reveals an unhappy childhood. Beware of what some call “overbearing verbosity.” Context matters. Disclosure has a commercial motive to boost sales, so it may feel transactional. An oversharing air hostess who leaks nervousness during turbulence fails to calm passengers.
  2. If in doubt, don’t. If you suspect you may be interpreted cynically or unfavorably, why disclose? Research finds that when the discloser holds status, vulnerability can reinforce trust rather than erode it. Not always. Rightly or wrongly, a struggling CEO signals weakness. In 2018, when Elon Musk told the New York Times he had just endured "the most difficult and painful year" of his career, Tesla shares fell 9 percent that day.
  3. Balance the trade-off. There’s no one-size-fits-all. Consider how much and when to share matters. Get it wrong and respect drains. Think of British Chancellor Rachel Reeves, who was seen crying in the House of Commons during Prime Minister's Questions in July 2025. Keir Starmer failed to back her. It was an involuntary disclosure that was rebuked. Although not always possible, we need to choose what we reveal.

Oversharing increases cancellation risk, so set boundaries. Share with those who respect you but pause with strangers, detractors, or casual observers. You can always say more tomorrow while you can never say less. A generation of open revealers or closed books isn’t the answer.

This is not a plea for repression but a call for caution and consideration in what you share, to whom, and when.

item.title: Watching the World Cup? It Might Be Good for Your Mental Health
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Watching the World Cup? It Might Be Good for Your Mental Health

If you are getting into the World Cup action, you are not alone.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Sports play a large role in our global community.
  • We are seeing this in the excitement around the World Cup.
  • Studies show that attending a sporting event can have mental health and wellness benefits.
People Soccer
Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Every four years, the world comes together to watch national teams compete in soccer’s biggest tournament. Whether you are a soccer fan or not, the spectacle is exciting and the talent is impressive. Soccer not your sport? You also have the option to watch Wimbledon, the oldest annual tennis tournament going on now in London. It is quieter, but no less exciting. The rest of the year, you have a panoply of sports to watch, both at the amateur and professional levels.

I am fortunate enough to be the primary therapist for the Washington Capitals, the National Hockey League team in DC. When I attend the games, I see how energized the fan base is. I also see the camaraderie of fans “high-fiving” and singing together. Intuitively, it makes sense that watching sports would be positive for one’s mental health, especially in person. Fortunately, we have research data that helps support this.

Multiple studies have explored the potential benefit of attending a sporting event. Helen Keyes, a cognitive psychologist at Anglia Ruskin University in England and colleagues found that attending a sporting event:

  • Improved self-reported anxiety
  • Decreased loneliness
  • Enhanced the sense that life is worth living

This finding is for attending both professional and amateur sporting events, which is encouraging, since current World Cup tickets are currently selling for well over $1,000.

But what about watching on television? It does not appear to reduce the sense of loneliness since it lacks the in-person bonding experience. However, some of the other benefits remain intact, such as positively impacting life satisfaction and well-being (Lera-López et al., 2021). This lowers the bar substantially as approximately 97% of Americans own at least one television, according to Nielsen research.

How can you take advantage of these wellness benefits? Consider the following:

  • Research the schedule for your local college or high school sports teams. Professional games are exhilarating but can be pricey.
  • Watch a few games on television of your favorite sport. Once you get to know some of the players and their personalities, it can be fun to root for them, even from the comfort of your couch.
  • Connect with friends who might have similar sports interests or team affiliations. This way, you can attend a game together or just share the camaraderie of watching your team on television.
  • Consider a World Cup “watch party.” Many cities are broadcasting the matches in downtown areas, block parties, or restaurants.

Sport is huge in America and across the world. Why not embrace the opportunity to join in the celebration and excitement of sports, be it local or global?

item.title: We Can (and Must) Find Meaning in Pain
item.description:
Resilience

We Can (and Must) Find Meaning in Pain

How to transform your suffering into growth.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Resilience is the strongest predictor of how we respond to adversity, regardless of what we face.
  • Spiritually intelligent people transform suffering by asking what pain is inviting them to learn.
  • Self-compassion creates the emotional safety needed to heal, adapt, and become more resilient.

In his famous Stanford commencement address, Steve Jobs described three defining disruptions in his life: dropping out of college, being fired from Apple, and receiving a cancer diagnosis. Rather than seeing these events as purely tragic, he positioned them as inflection points: moments that forced him to reflect and reframe his circumstances.

It’s an inspiring idea, but as a psychotherapist, I’ve encountered quite a few people who couldn’t find the same strength in adversity. Many (at least for the time being) faced failures and now feel primarily overwhelmed and defeated. They come to feel victimized by life, which leaves them completely disempowered.

What makes the difference?

Research Reveals: Resilience Is Key

Modern neuroscience confirms what spiritual traditions and psychological wisdom have long suggested: Stress and trauma themselves do not determine our fate, but rather, our response to them does.[i]

Stress can contribute to psychiatric, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders, but, of course, not everyone exposed to stress or trauma develops illness. The key determining factor is one’s resilience and choice of attitude, which is partially shaped by genetics, early life experiences, adult environment, health behaviors, and social context (as opposed to being a fixed trait that some possess and others lack). In exciting news, this means that, with conscious cultivation, resilience can be strengthened over time.

Improving our resilience helps us navigate life’s inevitable storms with greater ease, but it can also contribute to better emotional adjustment, stronger coping skills, and improved health outcomes.[ii]

Pain as a Teacher

My research into spiritually intelligent individuals[iii] suggests that one key factor is the ability to find meaning in suffering. My subjects don’t deny their pain. They allow it to become a source of insight, growth, and transformation. Thomas Edison captured this mindset when he said, “I have not failed. I’ve just found ten thousand ways that won’t work.”

Nearly all of the spiritually intelligent individuals I have studied spoke about their disappointment, loss, and suffering as opportunities to grow. One person explained, “Pain is my teacher. I allow myself to experience it fully and ask what it is inviting me to practice or learn.”

Rather than resisting or resenting difficulty, spiritually intelligent people practice openness to life as it unfolds. They begin by accepting reality, including their emotions, and then ask a powerful question: What is this situation calling forth in me?

By focusing on what can be developed rather than what has been lost, they expand their capacity to respond creatively rather than react defensively: true self-empowerment at work.

From Wounds to Purpose

To offer an example, I know a father whose teenage son was killed in an act of senseless violence. Rather than retreating into bitterness, he founded a nonprofit organization dedicated to reducing gang violence and providing alternative pathways for young men to gain status, belonging, and purpose.

article continues after advertisement

Such stories illustrate what psychiatrist Viktor Frankl observed after surviving Nazi concentration camps: “Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms—to choose one's own attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.”

Healing does not erase pain. But it can transform pain into compassion, wisdom, and service.

The Role of Self-Compassion

When facing difficulty, many people default to self-criticism or blame. We assume that something is wrong with reality or with us or that we have failed in some fundamental way.

Yet self-criticism rarely produces growth. More often, it produces paralysis.

Self-compassion, by contrast, creates the psychological safety necessary for transformation. The first step is simply acknowledging pain without judgment. Rather than suppressing or denying distress, we allow ourselves to feel it.

One simple practice is to place a hand on your heart and speak to yourself as you would to someone you love: This is difficult. It's normal, and many other people experience these kinds of challenges. You’re not alone. I am here going through this with you.

This act activates neural systems associated with safety, care, and emotional regulation, allowing the nervous system to shift from threat to restoration.

As the Buddha observed, “You can search the entire universe and not find a single being more worthy of loving kindness than yourself.”

A Practice for Finding Meaning in Difficulty

If you are currently facing a challenge, consider this simple reflection exercise:

Sit comfortably and bring attention to your breath. Notice your body. Invite yourself to become present.

Then ask yourself:

  • What is this situation calling forth in me?
  • What qualities would help me meet this challenge?
  • Do I already possess some of these qualities?
  • How might this experience contribute to my growth?

There are no right or wrong answers. The purpose is not to force meaning, but to remain open to uncovering it.

article continues after advertisement

From Victimhood to Agency

Whether meaning emerges immediately or only in hindsight, the act of searching for meaning itself can be transformative. When we assume that our experiences contain lessons, we shift from passive victims of circumstance to active participants in our own evolution.

Life becomes not merely a sequence of random events, but a journey of learning, growth, and unfolding purpose. Spiritual intelligence does not eliminate suffering. But it gives us the capacity to transform suffering into wisdom—and to emerge from difficulty not diminished, but rather, expanded.

item.title: Are You Ready for Your Prime Time?
item.description:
Midlife

Are You Ready for Your Prime Time?

Time may be getting shorter, but your prime may just be starting.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • People view midlife as a time of trouble and unhappiness, but it can also be viewed as a time of growth.
  • A new book challenges some of the predominant myths about midlife and shows how you can maximize your growth.
  • By findings ways to get gains to outweigh losses, your midlife can indeed become your “prime” time.

The essence of “midlife” may seem hard to grasp. Whether you’re in your 40s, 50s, or 60s, you may wonder how exactly to define your age group. Unfortunately, for better or worse, society seems pretty hung up on defining people in terms of their age. This can leave you confused, especially if—as many people will attest to— you don’t “feel” your age.

In a new book, Brandeis University psychologist Margie Lachman (2026) tackles this definitional question and more, showing readers that midlife has not only many possible meanings but also many possibilities. Primetime begins by questioning the very use of the term “middle” to capture what happens to people sometime between childhood and later adulthood. Indeed, as she notes, “midlife could use a better publicist.” After reading the book, you’ll understand why. Here, I’ll try to summarize just some of its main points.

Midlife as Prime Time

Because “middle” has so many negative connotations (“middle” seat of an airplane row, “middle” child, even “Middle Ages”), the term midlife is doomed from the get-go. But this doesn’t have to be the case. As Lachman points out, midlife is full of reasons to see it as a time of new possibilities for growth, change, and joy. And if you need to pin it down with a number, she suggests using the broad scope of 30s to 70s with the 40s and 50s as the central defining decades. You might not even know your midlife years until the end, of course. Thirty-five is the midlife point if you live to 70, but 50 is if you’re lucky enough to live to 100. It’s not worth getting too picky, though. You’re in midlife if you’re somewhere in the “middle.”

Unfortunately, many people look at midlife from the standpoint of the beginning of the end instead of the beginning of an exciting new phase. We’re conditioned to view aging from a negative lens due to the prominence of ageism, in which “old” is associated with loss. However, there are many gains in later life as well; Lachman calls the “framework of gains and losses” the “north star” of the book, based on her years of collecting data through the Midlife in the United States project (MIDUS). Here are some of her key points, as outlined in the opening chapter:

  1. Each of us is unique. People don’t universally go through life, including the later years.
  2. There is a seesaw effect. Within the same person, changes can occur at different rates.
  3. You are more flexible than you think. Development throughout life is marked by “plasticity,” or the ability to adapt.
  4. You can’t escape cause and effect. Your actions have consequences, so what you do now will affect what happens later. But, because of plasticity, you’re not doomed to play out a preordained life plan.
  5. Consider the context. You don’t age in a vacuum. What happens to people throughout life reflects their historical and social circumstances.

Tackling the Midlife Crisis Myth

If you’ve followed my own blog over the years, you’d know that the midlife crisis is the nemesis of virtually all personality researchers who study adulthood. Lachman, one of my (dare I say) co-conspirators in much of this, shows why with a convincing array of research, much of it based on MIDUS. Take a look at this quote:

Cultural shorthand and stereotypes like the ‘midlife crisis’ are a failure of curiosity, and they can lead to alienation, misunderstanding, and loneliness for everyone in the tick of midlife.

In other words, myths hurt. Even if you may come back with the retort that “reality hurts,” the exhaustive research she cites will show you that, though some people (maybe 10 or 20 percent) do hurt during midlife, the majority do just fine. And if you want to ensure that you end up on the winning side of the numbers, Lachman lists a few questions you can ask yourself. “What is going well and not well? Am I happy now with what I am doing?” “Where do I want to be in ten (five) years? What things do I want to be doing in ten (five) years?”

At the opposite end of the midlife crisis myth is the myth that personality doesn’t change at all in adulthood. Again, drawing from a host of empirical evidence, Lachman shows that whether it’s sense of identity or personality traits, people do change, and in fact “it gets better.”

The Nitty-Gritties: Intelligence, Health, Life Roles, and Resilience

It’s difficult to summarize an entire book in the space of this post, but I would like to tantalize you with a few specific reasons to take heart that life can and does get better.

Using that gains-and-losses framework, Lachman shows how, through the “Tale of Two Intelligences,” although your cognitive abilities are likely to show both patterns, the intelligence that counts (knowledge) is likely to gain even as your quick thinking may be less quick. Indeed, because gains can compensate for losses, “slower doesn’t necessarily mean less sharp.”

Compensation shows up as an important process in the health domain as well. Yes, our bodies change (and often in ways we don’t like), but “you can take action to mitigate unnecessary suffering.” Your behavior can account for, as she notes, 40 to 50 percent of the risk associated with death before age 75. One way to alter your behavior to keep that risk low is to exercise (as you undoubtedly know) and manage stress. If you’re not sure where to get started, Lachman provides some useful questions that can help you build “small successes” to produce large gains.

Work and family roles, where most people’s midlife energy is expended, become another area in which gains can outweigh losses with just a few manipulations on your part. Generativity, the sense of commitment to future generations, can help you focus attention away from your own problems and onto the activities that will give you not only a sense of meaning but also a foundation for your own future adaptation. When midlife throws you “for a loop,” you’ll have a “social convoy of support” that can carry you forward, in what Lachman calls “reaping the rewards.”

Finally, at any age—but especially in midlife—you encounter curveballs and wake-up calls; whether it’s someone getting sick, losing your job, or just dealing with stress, most people are able to turn on the power of resilience. By reframing these into “turning points,” you can go on to benefit, especially by making wise choices and “turning off autopilot,” or being more mindful about your daily life decisions. You’ll also have the advantage of recognizing “opportunities for happiness,” even in little ways. Finally, you may have to accept that you’ll often just have to “go with the flow” and not get too upset when some of those little things don’t turn out the way you wished.

To sum up, viewing the middle of your life as its prime doesn’t just have to be wishful thinking. You can find fulfillment at this or any age by recognizing that change is possible in midlife, before, and beyond.

item.title: Lithium, Bipolar Disorder, and Heat Sensitivity
item.description:
Bipolar Disorder

Lithium, Bipolar Disorder, and Heat Sensitivity

Personal Perspective: An Italy trip reminded me lithium can increase vulnerability to heat and dehydration.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Dizziness, nausea, grogginess, and twitching may signal lithium toxicity.
  • Travel, saunas, hot springs, and heat waves require a lithium safety plan.
  • Protecting stability means listening to your body, not pushing through.
Source: ap301805 / Pixabay

I recently traveled to Italy in the middle of a record heat wave. It was beautiful, memorable, and physically much harder than I expected.

Part of that was the heat itself. Part of it was the way travel quietly changes the body’s usual operating conditions. Air conditioning is not as prevalent in Italy as it is in much of the United States. Days that look reasonable on an itinerary can become a long chain of sun, walking, crowds, standing, sweating, and trying to keep up.

Our trip included hot springs and saunas. We went on a boat excursion. We toured the Vatican. These were extraordinary experiences. They were also, I now realize, exactly the kinds of conditions that can be risky for someone taking lithium.

At first, I did what many people do when they travel: I explained away the warning signs.

I was dizzy. I felt nauseated. I was extremely tired and groggy, not just “vacation tired,” but heavy and slowed down in a way that felt different. I noticed muscle twitches in my hands. Still, I blamed jet lag. I blamed the time change. I blamed disrupted sleep, changes in my schedule, different meals, too much walking, and the ordinary stress of being far from home.

Those explanations were not irrational. They were just incomplete.

Eventually, I realized what was happening: I was on lithium, and my body was struggling in the heat.

Lithium has been incredibly important in helping me manage bipolar disorder. For many people with bipolar disorder, lithium is not simply another pill in the medicine cabinet. It can be a foundation. It can reduce the risk of mania, depression, hospitalization, and the kind of life disruption that bipolar disorder can cause. In my own life, lithium has been part of the structure that allows me to work, write, teach, travel, and function.

So this is not an anti-lithium story.

It is a respect-lithium story.

Source: Ed Ergenzinger

Avoiding Lithium Toxicity While Traveling

Lithium is effective, but it has a narrow therapeutic range. That means the amount that helps and the amount that can become dangerous are closer together than we might wish. Dehydration, prolonged sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, illness, changes in salt intake, and certain medications can increase the risk of lithium toxicity. The Food and Drug Administration-approved prescribing information specifically warns that dehydration from sweating and changes in salt and fluid balance can increase the risk of lithium toxicity, and it emphasizes maintaining a normal diet with salt and adequate hydration.

That matters in ordinary life. It matters even more in extreme heat.

A sauna is not just relaxing if you take lithium. A hot spring is not just a vacation indulgence. A long walking tour in a crowded, hot city is not just sightseeing. Each of these can increase sweating, fluid loss, fatigue, and physiological stress.

Even something as seemingly innocuous as the fact that food is not salted in the same way many American foods are salted can cause problems. If you suddenly reduce your salt intake, your kidneys reabsorb sodium to maintain balance. But because lithium and sodium are chemically similar, lithium is also reabsorbed. This raises blood lithium levels and increases the risk of toxicity.

And the symptoms can be easy to misread.

Nausea can seem like something you ate. Dizziness can seem like heat exhaustion. Grogginess can seem like jet lag. Muscle twitching or tremor can seem like too much caffeine, not enough sleep, or just being worn out. Unfortunately, lithium toxicity can involve symptoms such as nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, tremor, poor coordination, confusion, and more serious neurological symptoms.

People with bipolar disorder often become experts at monitoring themselves. We learn to watch our sleep, our energy, our mood, our irritability, our impulsivity, and our stress. We know that travel can destabilize routines. We know that crossing time zones can interfere with sleep.

But competence can turn into overconfidence. I knew travel could affect my bipolar disorder. I was less attentive to how travel could affect the medication that keeps me from spinning into manic highs or depressive lows.

Planning Ahead for Travel on Lithium

The lesson is not that people taking lithium should never travel, never enjoy summer, or never go to Italy. The lesson is that lithium requires planning, especially when heat is part of the itinerary.

Before travel, especially to a hot climate, it is worth talking with your prescribing clinician about hydration, salt intake, warning signs, whether blood levels should be checked, and what to do if symptoms appear. Do not stop or change lithium on your own. But do ask for a plan. Ask what symptoms should prompt a call, an urgent care visit, or an emergency evaluation. Ask whether hot springs, saunas, strenuous walking tours, anti-inflammatory medications such as ibuprofen, or gastrointestinal illness should change the plan.

During travel, “drink water” is necessary but not always sufficient. People on lithium generally need consistent fluid intake and a consistent diet, including sodium, unless a clinician has advised otherwise. In practical terms, that may mean carrying electrolyte drinks, taking cooling breaks seriously, avoiding unnecessary sauna or hot-spring exposure in extreme weather, building rest into the day, and avoiding the urge to treat heat symptoms as something to power through.

There is a psychological piece here as well. Many of us who live with bipolar disorder do not want to feel medically fragile. We want to be spontaneous. We want to participate. We want to say yes to the tour, the hot spring, or the hike.

But self-protection is not fragility—it's what allows the life we want to continue.

My trip to Italy was wonderful. I'm grateful for it. But I also came home with a renewed respect for the medication that helps keep me well.

Lithium has helped give me a life I once feared I might not have. A life in which I can travel, work, write, teach, love, and participate in the world. That is why I will remember that the medication that has been my salvation comes with real risks that change with context.

item.title: Why Modern Couples Need Rituals More Than Ever
item.description:
Relationships

Why Modern Couples Need Rituals More Than Ever

Observances and rituals give love a form it does not have to reinvent.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Many couples are not under-communicating. They are overburdened and need forms they can return to.
  • Not every ritual should be a conversation. For some partners, verbal check-ins become another test of fluency.
  • A good ritual does not have to be dramatic. The test is whether it still happens when the feeling isn't there.
  • Rituals do not make the partner everything. They protect the partner from having to be everything.

The marriage has become the village.

Every institution around marriage has become smaller. Marriage has become larger.

We did not become less ritualistic. We became responsible for inventing our own rituals.

A partner is now expected to be a lover, best friend, co-parent, confidant, emotional regulator, witness, social companion, and source of meaning. This can sound romantic — you are my person, you are my home — until the weight of it becomes impossible to miss.

A partner cannot be the whole ecosystem.

Many modern couples are not under-communicating. They are overburdened. They talk constantly: in the kitchen, by text, between meetings, while one person is half inside a phone and the other is trying not to sound disappointed. For many couples who work from home, the pressure is not metaphorical: the home is also the office; there is nowhere for a mood to go. Even making toast becomes a tiny referendum on the relationship. Do I offer some? Interrupt? Stay quiet?

The words are already there. What is missing is form: something a relationship can lean on without having to explain itself from scratch. Research confirms what practice shows: couples with rituals tend toward more satisfaction and more commitment. A couple cannot live on intensity alone. It needs rhythm.

When Words Become the Wrong Tool

Some rituals are conversations. A check-in I use with couples sets aside time to notice what the week would otherwise erase: the errand handled without being asked, the text that landed at the right moment, the pressure removed before it became another fight. But not every ritual should be a conversation.

For some partners, especially those who are less verbal or speaking in a second language, a sentence stem is not an invitation. It is an audition. The more you ask partners to perform closeness, the more the one who is good with words is advantaged. A ritual should not become another test of fluency. Some couples do not need another summit about their relationship. They need the relationship to keep happening.

The Latte

I know a couple who have been married for decades. Every morning, without discussion or ceremony, he goes downstairs, makes her a latte — not coffee, a latte, exactly the way she likes it — and brings it up to her in bed. That is how she starts her day. No processing required.

Think of an old Etch A Sketch. Whatever got drawn the night before — the argument, the silence, the thing that was said and cannot be unsaid — does not disappear exactly, but it loosens its grip. The screen clears enough to begin again.

article continues after advertisement

The latte creates something harder to name than repair: A form of return. The morning has a way of starting again. Yesterday's mood does not automatically own the new day. The latte says, without saying it: we are still here.

In a long marriage, that may be the most important message there is. Not the most dramatic. The most true. Some things in relationships are repaired not by analysis, but by return.

The Walk

Another couple I know has the usual friction: irritation, patience worn thin, small misreads, nothing that puts the relationship in question. They are not walking because nothing is wrong. What is notable is not what they overcome. It is what they return to.

Every morning: espresso, shoes, out the door. No one waits for a conversation to start. They walk side by side, down the street, around some hills, toward the beach. Face-to-face can become a deposition: two people with nowhere to look but at each other, the relationship the only thing in the room. Side by side is different. Their eyes are outward. They share the same water, the same dogs, the same ordinary theater of the morning.

Some couples do not need another conversation about the relationship. They need to be next to each other in life. They do not step on each other. Sometimes they talk. Sometimes they do not. They finish the walk anyway. By the time they turn back, the day has its shape.

The Question That Matters

Rituals do not make the partner everything. They protect the partner from having to be everything.

The test is Tuesday morning, the night after the argument, the day nobody feels generous. Does the day begin differently because of it? Does the evening end with something other than drift? Does it still happen when the feeling isn't there?

A latte. A walk. Ten minutes outside before dark. A weekly check-in that starts with what went right. They are small by design. They have to be repeatable.

Neighborhoods, families, friendships, religious communities, civic life — more of what once lived there now comes home.

The marriage has become the village.

But love cannot carry that weight alone. It needs structure. It needs rhythm. It needs a way back.

item.title: Why Music Makes Us So Nostalgic
item.description:
Nostalgia

Why Music Makes Us So Nostalgic

Music has a particular power to evoke nostalgia and send us back in time. This is why.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Listening to nostalgia-evoking music can strengthen our connections with our past, present, and future selves.
  • Nostalgic music can help us process challenging emotions and reintegrate positive states into the present.
  • Music-evoked nostalgia has been linked with significant enhancements in memory.
Source: Robertobinetti70/iStock

Music holds the power of a time machine. Imagine you have your music library on shuffle: One moment you’re listening to a new hit, and the next, you’re transported back in time by a song from your past. Overcome with bittersweet reminiscence of a younger you, both your volume and nostalgia are dialled up to ten.

Of all the five senses, hearing—namely, our ability to recognize the rhythmic patterns in a song—is identified as one of the strongest triggers of nostalgia. Research on music-evoked nostalgia has linked this experience with enhanced inspiration, optimism, social bonding, memory, life-meaning, and self-continuity; awareness of and connectedness to our past, present, and future selves.

Self-Continuity from a Song

Self-continuity is, in my opinion, one of the most beautiful features of nostalgia-evoking music. In my therapy room, I help guide clients in building relationships with past versions of themselves that have been left behind and/or are subconsciously running their lives today. Just as these therapeutic interventions help collapse space and time in the client’s internal system, so too can music. Modern research on self-continuity reveals that individuals who experience nostalgia from listening to music feel closer to their past selves and have a deeper awareness of traits they’d like to release or maintain across their lifespan.

Source: PeopleImages/iStock

For instance, consider one of your nostalgic shuffle-songs from the example above. If this tune was from your childhood, memories of a younger you might highlight the importance of play and presence. If the song reminds you of your teens, you might feel excitement towards a version of yourself who experienced love for the first time, or compassion towards the you who was struck by heartbreak. Or say the song is from your adult life, you may be taken back to the first dance at your wedding or a cherished moment as a new parent.

That’s the beauty of music-evoked nostalgia; it knows no timeline, and it invites us to slow down, reflect, and even sing along.

Getting "In Tune" with Big Emotions

Listening to nostalgic music can also help us process more uncomfortable emotions such as sadness, anger, grief, and anxiety.

Consider a nostalgic song that evokes some of these challenging feelings. Maybe this song leads you to yearn for "the good old days," and, likely, there are some unprocessed emotions tied to this sense of longing. This is when the "bitter" half of nostalgia’s "bittersweetness" is triggered. Interestingly, science shows how embracing this experience can help with emotional processing and even transport that past sense of contentment and safety into the present.

article continues after advertisement
Source: MajaPhoto/iStock

For example, a research study on music-evoked nostalgia measured what types of songs Spotify listeners favoured during the COVID-19 pandemic. Data from almost 17 trillion song plays across Europe revealed a significant spike in nostalgic music consumption during the first wave of pandemic lockdowns, compared with before and after. This fascinating data supports the idea that music is always there to call us back from hardships to times that felt simpler, freer, and likely more exciting.

Nostalgia can be painful, but it typically only hurts when we feel disconnected from these past positive experiences. But here’s the good news: Old music is an invitation to reintegrate those experiences into your present-day life.

Consider what you might be missing from your life right now, which you long for. Meaning? Freedom? Romance? Play? Fitness? Creativity? Was there a time in your life when you were immersed in these experiences? Can you find a song you enjoyed listening to around that same time?

If you can, that's wonderful, and I encourage you to play that tune and let each note resonate—no distractions. What we’re doing is activating your long-term memory and allowing it to prime your mind with the sensations you wish to bring forth into the now.

Your Autobiographical Playlist

Modern science shows how one of the most marked benefits of music-evoked nostalgia is enhanced memory recall, memory vividness, and autobiographical memory, for both younger and older adults. In other words, every time our "nostalgic music time machine" lets us relive past experiences, those memories are reinforced in our brains. With mindful awareness of each note, beat, pitch, rhythm, and tempo, we are quite literally bridging the perceived gaps in space and time.

Source: Photodjo/iStock

For those who struggle with memory recall—specifically, individuals diagnosed with dementia—nostalgic music has been shown to improve state-level well-being by accessing joyful memories from across their lifespan. As such, nostalgia-evoking music is gaining attention as a potential non-pharmacological intervention for individuals with dementia and as a potential preventive measure against memory impairment.

When we consider the vast spread of music that has touched us throughout our lives, we give ourselves the opportunity to feel connected to every single version of ourselves; then, now, and to come. Music has the power to place us at the centre of our little universes whilst also helping us feel connected to one another and to forces far greater than us. With that, I invite you to board your nostalgic music time machine: press play, take pause, and let the songs rewind you into reminiscence.

item.title: Life Lessons From a Roman Philosopher
item.description:
Philosophy

Life Lessons From a Roman Philosopher

Is skepticism a good guide for living well?

Posted June 30, 2026

Review of How to Be a (Happy) Skeptic: The Power of Doubt in a Meaningful Life. By Massimo Pigliucci. Tarcher. 333 pp. $32.

“We should not be too confident in our belief in anything,” Marcus Tullius Cicero, a statesman and philosopher in the Roman Republic, often declared. Nonetheless, Massimo Pigliucci points out that Cicero maintained we should embrace beliefs not as absolute truths, but as logically consistent propositions that conform to the best available evidence and are subject to revision in light of new information.

Source: Gordon Johnson/Pixabay

In How to Be a (Happy) Skeptic, Pigliucci (a professor of philosophy at the City College of New York and author, among other books, of How to Be a Stoic) uses Cicero as his guide in an examination of the role curiosity and reason can play in laying the foundations of a good life. Part biography of an iconic figure in Western civilization, part history of the last days of the Roman Republic, and part self-help primer, his book is informative and engaging.

Pigliucci acknowledges that “even the best philosophical arguments sometimes fail to convince people,” especially when they concern “deeply felt issues.” But he does not adequately address how often emotion trumps reason in shaping beliefs and behavior. “Contrary to what one often hears,” he writes, without much elaboration, “we are not helpless in the face of our emotions, even strong ones.” Along with Cicero, he asserts that those who cannot bear pain “cannot achieve worthwhile things,” while those who accept it “as a fact of life often discover that they are more than a match for it.” "Which category would you rather belong to?” he asks, as if “the right answer” is all individuals need to make a choice and act on it. And Pigliucci endorses Cicero’s recommendation to accept death as inevitable and refuse to give it further thought, because it is inevitable.

That said, How to Be a (Happy) Skeptic contains lots of useful and practical advice. Stoicism, Pigliucci indicates, has shaped cognitive behavioral therapy. Stoics identified what psychologist Daniel Kahneman called “fast” (subconscious and instinctive) and “slow” (conscious, deliberate, and often more accurate) thinking. And slow thinking prompted Ulysses, who wanted to hear the song of the sirens even though he realized his curiosity might be fatal, to order his crew to tie him to the mast of their ship, ears unencumbered.

Convinced that how we confront adversity, challenges, and setbacks shapes our responses to them – a fundamental precept of rational emotive behavior therapy – Pigliucci recommends “reframing” issues, “a powerful and seriously underestimated ability common to all humankind.” When his daughter died in childbirth, Cicero, he reveals, may have been the first person to write letters “of self-consolation,” a practice recommended by CBT professionals to their clients in the form of meditative journals addressing themselves in the second person in non-emotional language. Like the Stoics, he notes, CBT practitioners also warn against “catastrophizing” about real or feared calamities. Here again, a caveat is in order: The Epicurean recommendation of immersion in “something pleasurable” to ward off grief may be “sound,” but it is much easier said than done.

article continues after advertisement

Pigliucci also provides a vocabulary well-suited to open-minded inquiry. A hypothetical or conditional imperative, he suggests, differs from a categorical imperative (like the Ten Commandments) because it is not absolute. Emphasizing the importance to our species of empathy, cooperation and reciprocity, primatologists characterize human beings (and some mammals) as “obligatorily gregarious,” inclined to practice “reciprocal altruism and punish “free riders.” Pigliucci also stresses what he regards as an urgent need to focus on “actual, not virtual friendships” before cementing what may appear to be at first blush a profound relationship.

Pigliucci recognizes, of course, that reading the classics in general, or Cicero in particular, will not by itself lead to a life well lived. Only knowledge that is internalized and followed by action “will change anything.”

That said, ancient wisdom, with all its flaws, is by no means a bad way to start “the project of self-improvement” in an age of “artificial intelligence and instant gratification.”

item.title: Caregiving During Retirement: A Likelihood for Many of Us
item.description:
Caregiving

Caregiving During Retirement: A Likelihood for Many of Us

We frequently become caregivers during retirement, and it isn't easy.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us will become voluntary or involuntary caregivers during our retirement years.
  • Comprehensive retirement planning now needs to include probable caregiving responsibilities.
  • Caregiving commonly leads to financial challenges as well as physical and mental health complications.

One recognized challenge of retirement is that it often overlaps with other major life events, and there may be two, three, or four major changes occurring simultaneously. One of the most common is caregiving.

A 2025 report co-authored by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 55 percent of caregivers are aged 50 years and older (with 22 percent being aged 65 years and older). Regardless of this finding, few of us plan on becoming a caregiver for a loved one during our retirement years unless we already have this role.

Caregiving currently isn't part of traditional retirement planning, even though one's aspirations for this phase of life, such as travel and a far-less hectic schedule, can implode when the need arises. Indeed, our ideal of retirement may be placed on permanent hold; the above study found a significant number of caregivers were forced to delay retirement.

Let's begin with a comprehensive definition of caregiving articulated by Triantafillou et al. (2010), who note it consists of a close relationship with the care receiver, little to no professional training, no payment for services, a wide range of caregiving duties, no official hours (never really off duty), and little social recognition of this important role.

Who are we caring for? The most common persons requiring our assistance are parents, spouses, siblings, and, increasingly, friends (particularly those who are single and childless). Some of us will be caregivers multiple times, such as caring for aging parents during our middle-age years and then supporting a spouse or sibling in our retirement. We may even have to assist multiple care receivers simultaneously.

Research on the Stress Associated With Caregiving

Let's be clear that caring for a loved one can be a satisfying experience; it offers many emotional rewards and is a meaningful way of honoring past service the caregiver received from the person now needing care. Still, there is abundant research about the stress associated with caregiving, and several recurrent themes are noted.

First, there are financial implications. In their article “Who Is Taking Care of the Caregiver?” Sullivan and Miller (2015) conclude, "Often the needs caused by the chronic illness assume financial priority in a family.” According to the AARP report, one-third of caregivers stopped saving money, and 24 percent had used up short-term savings. Others reported taking on more debt. Half of employed caregivers reported arriving late, leaving early, or taking time off to meet caregiving obligations.

There are also physical health implications. Caregiving is physically taxing, particularly when a care receiver is bedbound and needs care in the form of bathing, dressing, and toileting. Caregiving work is also becoming more complex; more than 70 percent of family caregivers are providing care for an individual who has two or more health conditions. They are also providing care for longer periods of time (a third of family caregivers are providing care for someone for five years or more).

In spite of receiving little to no training, caregivers are navigating complex medical and nursing tasks that in the not-too-distant past would have been managed in acute care settings. Additionally, they assume non-medical tasks—in particular, taking over the financial responsibilities of the care receiver. When we then add interrupted sleep, communicating with professionals and family, monitoring the patient, and being available 24 hours per day, we can understand how draining this can be. As a result, one of the greatest risks for caregivers is becoming ill themselves.

In a 2020 review of literature on caregiver burden, Liu et al. determined that caregivers often neglect to take care of themselves (even when sick) and rarely seek medical help even though more than 50 percent had chronic health issues (such as heart problems and hypertension). Older caregivers face even more challenges due to their own age-related concerns. In an article in the Journal of the American Medical Association, Adelman et al. (2014) summarized available research and concluded, “Caregivers become the invisible patient.”

Mental Health Implications of Caregiving

Finally, there are mental health implications. The majority of studies find caregiving negatively impacts mental health. Caregivers frequently experience a reduction in social activities, increased levels of stress and distress, lower levels of life satisfaction, and more psychological symptoms, including depression, anxiety, guilt, worry, and anger. In the aforementioned AARP report, isolation and feeling alone were frequent occurrences.

As a succinct summary of the above caregiving research, consider the conclusion of Jason Resendez (2025), president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, who states that the healthcare system is engaging in borderline exploitation of family caregivers.

Three Approaches to Prepare for Caregiving During Retirement

Obviously, this is not how most people envision retirement, yet it will be a reality for many of us. What then should we be doing to prepare for caregiving during retirement? A detailed answer is beyond the space limitations of a blog post, but as an overview, there are three primary approaches: (1) emergency planning, (2) education, and (3) financial planning.

Begin by ascertaining that you have critical information for the persons most likely to need your care; this includes power of attorney and medical proxy documentation, insurance information, and passwords for cell phones and computers (since so much of our financial life is now done online). A medical emergency or catastrophic accident can occur at any time, and a lack of these details results in unnecessary challenges and stress.

It is also important to be aware of the most common supportive strategies for caregivers. Sörensen et al. (2002) evaluated these strategies and separated them into distinct categories: education, peer and professional support, respite care, and therapy. Specific interventions include:

  • Becoming educated about the particular condition(s) afflicting a loved one.
  • Engaging in self-care and practicing healthy living.
  • Talking to your employer. As state and national efforts belatedly catch up to the new realities of retirement, some employers have taken the lead by implementing policies that support caregivers, such as working from home, flexible shifts, and reduced work hours that do not negatively impact one's career.
  • Staying proactively social, including with friends and other family members.
  • Attending support groups, both professional and peer-led.
  • Asking for help and accepting it when offered.
  • Utilizing therapy to share emotions that can’t be vented with other people, problem solve, and even gain new perspectives.
  • Using supportive technology to lighten the load, including emergency response systems and home monitoring devices.
  • Taking caregiver holidays. This intervention engages the care receiver away from home, including adult day care or a temporary stay in a skilled nursing facility.

The final consideration is the impact of caregiving on our financial resources in retirement. According to the AARP in its 2021 Caregiving Out-of-Pocket Costs Study, 78 percent of caregivers report having out-of-pocket expenses as a result of caregiving, most notably spending one quarter (26 percent) of their income on caregiving activities. Many of us will need to recalculate what our retirement spending may be based on this finding and adjust accordingly.

To conclude, many describe caregiving as one of the most rewarding and even sacred roles of their lives, but it remains inescapably stressful. Recognizing this, we can begin to factor caregiving into our retirement planning, particularly its impact on financial assets, relationship dynamics, health, and how we will spend our time. And for those who are already caregivers, please make use of the above recommendations to minimize personal health risks and their subsequent impact on care receivers.

item.title: Why Athletes Need Yoga
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Why Athletes Need Yoga

How does yoga support athletic performance and athlete well-being?

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Yoga is connection to the life force—your own, your teammates’, and your competitors’.
  • Athletes don't need anything for a yoga practice outside of their intention to be present here and now.
  • The practice of full presence is connected to higher performance, empirically and anecdotally.

Any gold medalist will tell you that at the highest levels of sport, you’re often training for that 1 percent edge over yourself and your past performances and over your competition, who are also taking exquisite care with the finest details of training.

It’s a lot to manage. On top of managing emotions and expectations and relationships. On top of managing everything else life throws at you.

Yoga is about not-managing. Which can be scary for athletes. Terrifying, even. And maybe even sounds contradictory to some research about the importance of attentional control in sport and high-performance endeavors. But only on the surface. Instead of holding the reins on our attention so tightly, yoga asks us to allow whatever is present to be present so that we don’t waste energy suppressing thoughts or feelings we wish didn’t have. Which matters massively for athletic performance.

A yoga practice doesn’t have to mean the poses you see on Instagram. It doesn’t have to mean any poses at all. A yoga practice can look a lot of different ways that may or may not involve things you do with your physical body.

You don’t need a mat. You don’t need a thing, outside of your intention, the intention to be here, now, with what is, in this moment. And maybe you chose to move your body in this moment. Maybe you choose to attend to your breath. There are many different ways to do this, and we’ll talk more about some of these possible practices in a future post, but for now, let’s talk a little more about what research has shown about the connection between yoga practice and athletic performance.

There are at least six interrelated and empirically validated mechanisms through which yoga improves sport performance. They are:

1. Performance Enhancement and Recovery

Studies have demonstrated that regular yoga practice can improve flexibility, balance, and core stability—all crucial elements for most sports. For example, a 2020 study in the Journal of Sports Science and Medicine found that collegiate athletes who practiced yoga twice weekly for 10 weeks showed significant improvements in balance scores and flexibility compared to a control group.

2. Mental Focus and Stress Management

Research indicates that yoga’s mindfulness components help athletes manage competition-related stress and anxiety, with sleep quality and emotional regulation during high-stakes events. Yoga also helps to decrease cortisol and optimize metabolic states. Anecdotally, Olympic athletes who have incorporated yoga into their training have also reported better emotional regulation during high-pressure situations and improved sleep quality.

3. Injury Prevention

Multiple studies have shown that yoga can help reduce injury rates among athletes. This is attributed to improved body awareness (proprioception) and better movement patterns. Research with professional basketball players found that those who practiced yoga had fewer overuse injuries over a season compared to non-practitioners.

4. Breathing and Recovery

The pranayama (breathing) practices in yoga have been shown to enhance respiratory efficiency and recovery. Studies with endurance athletes have found improved VO2 max and reduced recovery time between training sessions for those practicing specific yoga breathing techniques.

5. Flow State Activation and Energy Management

Every task in sport requires a specific level of activation for each athlete, and each athlete must discover their own “optimal” level of activation for the tasks they must perform. They also need a routine to efficiently guide their bodies to that level of activation. Yoga helps athletes learn about their nervous system and what they need for increased or decreased activation, and how to navigate that activation smoothly and directly.

6. Imagery and Neural Networks

As discussed in a previous article, imagery changes your brain. Imagined movement activates the same regions of your brain as actual movement, strengthening neural networks for enhanced efficiency during physical m movement in complex and unpredictable environments. Yoga supports seeing from within—a clear and vivid understanding of how your body moves and how your nervous system responds to movement, enhancing your imagery practice. And studies have shown that consistent imagery practice can improve an athlete’s performance by 20 to 25 percent. That’ll go a long way toward the 1 percent edge you’ll need for your gold medal.

Now about that “letting go.” There are many ways to practice yoga. Yoga is not the poses. It’s not a YouTube channel. It is not the hashtag-yoga photos you see on social media.

Yoga is a connection to the life force—your life force, your teammates’, and your competitors’. It is a connection to your inner wisdom. Wisdom that is always there within you, unbreakably. But our minds and what we have to manage—not to mention the stimuli and stresses of modern life—are often so active that it can be hard to access this inner wisdom.

So yoga is there and has been there for thousands of years to help us find what we need to let go and listen. To let go and fully release yourself into the process of experiencing who you are—which may be a gold medalist! And the benefits are much (much!) larger—and far more precious—than any medal or outcome.

item.title: RFK Jr. Launches Dangerous Mental Health Plan
item.description:
Psychiatry

RFK Jr. Launches Dangerous Mental Health Plan

HHS promotes stigma in effort to combat the “overuse” of psychiatric medicine.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • A new U.S. federal plan focuses on combating the “overprescription” of psychiatric medications.
  • Public figures have contributed to the persistent stigma of taking what are often life-saving medications.
  • The government can provide meaningful help to those with serious mental illness by funding supportive housing.

In May 2026, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a plan to address the country’s mental health crisis. It focuses on combating the “overprescription” of psychiatric medications as part of an effort to “shift the standard of care toward prevention, transparency and a more holistic approach to mental health.”

Source: Bermix Studio / Unsplash

As a mental health attorney and advocate who, for decades, has guided families of loved ones with serious mental illness and substance use disorders, I believe that it is dangerous for RFK Jr. to put forth this idea. While overprescription can occur across medical specialties, medication compliance is particularly vital to those with serious mental health diagnoses. It is critical to their ability to stabilize and lead fulfilling independent lives and, unfortunately, already presents challenges due to how mental illness often impedes individuals’ insight.

Impact of Public Figures on the Stigma of Psychiatric Medication Use

Historically, the complexities of mental illness have not deterred public figures from weighing in on psychiatric treatment. In 2005, Tom Cruise criticized fellow actor Brooke Shields on network television for sharing how antidepressants helped her overcome postpartum depression. In 2022, then Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene blamed the Highland Park Fourth of July shootings on antidepressants and SSRIs, despite a total lack of evidence. These and other incidents contribute to the persistent stigma of taking what are often life-saving medications.

Still, RFK Jr.’s announcement is part of a shift that is unusually hazardous for individuals and families impacted by mental illness. He is speaking from a position of not just influence but very real, federal authority. His plan has the potential to have a chilling impact on prescribers throughout the country and speaks to the need for a renewed focus on expertise as well as on-the-ground experience throughout all layers of government.

Those of us who are deeply enmeshed in the day-to-day realities of mental illness understand the recklessness of RFK Jr.’s plan as well as the lack of necessity behind it. To illustrate, under current mental health law, hospitalized psychiatric patients have the protection of due process. If they refuse medications, hospitals can only force compliance by obtaining a court order and proving their lack of capacity to consent to or refuse treatment.

Instead of propagating ill-advised ideas, the federal government can provide meaningful help to this vulnerable population and their families by funding supportive housing for those with serious mental health diagnoses—an urgent priority. Without appropriate housing options, many individuals will never experience the stability needed to allow their treatments to have the intended impact, a reality that often falsely convinces people that medications are not effective.

Advocating for Medical Expertise and Appropriate Treatment in Mental Healthcare

Mental illness is an illness. It is a medical condition, even if termed mental illness, the treatment for which should never be influenced by those with no expertise or training. We must collectively keep such interference at bay and continue the use of safe, effective medications and other treatments that help individuals stabilize, recover, and live productive lives along with their loved ones.
